title: Renew the old
hookLine: Rav Kook taught that the old should be renewed and the new made holy
carry: renew the old, bless the new
tomorrow: can a hope for gentleness reach all the way to the animals?

lines: A RECIPE CARD, TEXTED TO EVERYONE.
OLD AND NEW ON ONE STOVETOP.
THE OLD RENEWED, THE NEW MADE HOLY.
cards: A grandmother's recipe card, splattered and soft at the corners, gets photographed and texted to the whole family, then made with oat milk because a cousin can't do dairy. Old and new, on one stovetop.
Rabbi Abraham Isaac Kook, known as Rav Kook, a rabbi and mystic in the Land of Israel, answered the question in one short Hebrew line: ha-yashan yitchadesh, ve-he-chadash yitkadesh.
The old will be renewed, and the new will be made holy.

teach.b: So, what do you do with something old that still matters? Rav Kook's answer runs both ways. The old doesn't get frozen behind glass or thrown out; it gets renewed, made alive again for new people in a new time.

teach.h: THE NEW, LIFTED AND GIVEN A PLACE.
teach.b: And the new doesn't get feared or swallowed whole; it gets made holy, lifted up and given a place. He refused to choose between the house of study and the changing world outside it.
Now a neighbor tradition, in its own words. In the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus ends a run of parables with a picture.
In the King James Version, every scribe instructed unto the kingdom of heaven "is like unto a man that is an householder, which bringeth forth out of his treasure things new and old."

A house with a treasure room, and someone who knows when to bring out each thing. Here's the shared ground: neither one picks only the old or only the new. Both trust a person to carry the two together.

And the honest difference. Rav Kook speaks of the Torah's life renewed among his own people. In Matthew the treasure is the teaching of the kingdom of heaven, which Christians hear as the teaching of Jesus.

teach.h: RENEW THE OLD, BLESS THE NEW.
teach.b: And the verbs differ. Matthew's householder brings things out as they are. Rav Kook asks that both be changed: the old renewed, the new made holy.

how: Rav Kook's line 'the old will be renewed and the new will be made holy' is quoted in Jewish schools and study halls, and his letters and essays are studied as a way of bringing tradition and the modern world together.

o: make old things alive again, and make new things holy
keep everything old exactly the way it always was
replace old customs with new ones as the times change

games.q: old and new, two ways — tap the pairs.
p: the new will be made holy
brings out things new and old
wouldn't choose between old and new

s: Rav Kook taught that new ideas are a threat to keep out
the new will be made holy: lifted up and given a place.
Matthew pictures a householder bringing out things new and old
Matthew 13:52: out of his treasure things new and old.
Rav Kook's line and Matthew's householder say exactly the same thing
the householder brings both out as they are; Rav Kook asks that both be changed, and their treasures differ.

games.q: your family's Passover seder has run the same way for years, and your little cousins are bored. what would Rav Kook's line suggest?
o: keep the old words, and find new ways to bring them alive.
drop the old parts the kids find boring, and start fresh.
change nothing; tradition only works if it never adapts.
games.why: the old will be renewed, and the new made holy: not frozen, not thrown out, but brought alive for new people.

practice: Find one old thing within reach that still matters: a worn book, a tool, a photo, a mug from someone you love. Give it one small act of renewal during the sit: wipe it clean, smooth a page, set it where you'll see it.
As you do, ask what new day it could belong to.

carryVoice: Your line: renew the old, bless the new, and carry both out of the same treasure room. Shalom.
